title: WHAT IF MARS WENT SILENT FOR 100 SECONDS?

segments.line: For one hundred seconds, a rover on Mars heard nothing.
Its own radio had gone quiet.
And the brain on board noticed every missing beat.
Twenty-five in a row, and it pulled the plug.
This is NASA's Perseverance, and it is still in trouble today.
So what if you were the one stuck inside it?
Here is the rule. Your radio must say hello to your brain.
A little ping, again and again, about every four seconds.
Each ping resets a counter inside the main computer.
Ping, reset. Ping, reset. You barely notice it.
But if the pings stop, the counter keeps climbing.
Hit the limit, and the computer assumes the radio is dead.
Thirty October. Your alarm goes off, you power on for the day.
Your main radio is supposed to wake up with you.
It doesn't send a single ping.
One missed. Then five. Then ten.
You can't feel it, but your computer is counting.
At twenty-five, that is about a hundred seconds of silence.
Your computer does not panic. It follows a script.
Step one. Power off the radio that stopped talking.
Step two. Swap to the backup radio, an identical twin.
Step three. Shut everything non-essential down. Safe mode.
Cameras off. Arm still. Wheels still. You wait.
Ground teams on Earth bring the rover back out of it.
Good news. You're awake, and the backup radio works.
Then the engineers read the data, and find a second problem.
The backup is only transmitting at about half its expected power.
So now both radios are in doubt.
NASA stops using either one until it is sure they're safe.
A radio you cannot trust is worse than silence.
So how do you talk to Earth with no relay radio?
Normally, your radios hand data up to an orbiter overhead.
The orbiter has a big dish and a quick path to Earth.
That is the fast lane for pictures, and lots of them.
With both relay radios parked, you have one option left.
Shout straight at Earth, using your big white dish.
It is called the high-gain antenna, on the X-band.
NASA's Deep Space Network dishes on Earth listen for you.
The catch. The data rate is significantly lower.
It is like going from fibre broadband to a dial-up modem.
So you do the sensible thing. You save the bandwidth.
Everything left in the pipe goes to diagnostics. Not science.
Science and instrument work are paused.
No new pictures. The raw image feed on the website goes quiet.
For a camera-mad rover, that is a very long weekend.
And the rover is not the only machine in trouble.
Meet Mars Odyssey, the orbiter that carries the rover's mail.
It launched in April two thousand one.
It reached Mars orbit that October.
It was designed to work for just over two and a half years.
It has now orbited Mars for twenty-five years.
Longer than any other mission has ever worked at the Red Planet.
It mapped the whole surface, and found buried ice a metre down.
It also relayed the first pictures from four landers.
Phoenix. Spirit. Opportunity. Curiosity.
So when Odyssey stumbles, the whole Mars network feels it.
Between the fourth and sixth of November, Odyssey went into safe mode.
Engineers found a reaction wheel had stopped spinning.
Think of reaction wheels as the spacecraft's steering.
Speed one up or slow it down, and the whole craft turns.
That keeps its solar panels pointed at the Sun.
Odyssey carries four wheels.
One of them already died back in twenty thirteen.
Now a second one has stopped. That leaves two.
And the rule is simple. You need at least three.
Without three, you steer with thrusters alone.
Thrusters burn hydrazine, and Odyssey has been up there a long time.
After twenty-five years, the tank is far from full.
The team estimates enough fuel to steer alone for one to two months.
That is a clock, and nobody can pause it.
They are still refining that estimate, so the number could move.
Meanwhile the rover's backup mail carrier is limping.
Two sick machines, on one planet, in the same fortnight.
Remember the heartbeat? Mission control is listening to a heartbeat too.
Remember the heartbeat? Mission control is listening to a heartbeat too.
So the teams run tests. One at a time, carefully.
They command the stuck wheel to move.
And in one test, it does.
Whether it is truly recoverable, they don't know yet.
Odyssey is out of safe mode, but its science is still off.
The goal is science and relay back by late November.
Perseverance hopes to be back doing science by the end of the month.
So back to the hundred seconds of silence.
The rover did not break. It did what it was built to do.
It noticed the silence, swapped, and protected itself.
Out there, listening for a heartbeat is how you stay alive.
Which would you fix first, the rover or the orbiter?
Tell me in the comments.
Tomorrow: what if tonight's supermoon hung even closer?
